newsitem.title: USA: SEC targets Merrill Lynch for Orange County deals.
newsitem.headline: SEC targets Merrill Lynch for Orange County deals.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission has informed Merrill Lynch & Co. that it intends to recommend enforcement action against the firm for alleged disclosure violations in Orange County, Calif., bond offerings, attorneys involved in the case said on Thursday.
Merrill Lynch received a so-called Wells notice several months ago, said the attorneys, who asked not to be identified.

The Wells notice indicates that the SEC is considering taking action against Merrill Lynch for alleged disclosure violations in offering statements for bonds that were issued by the county and underwritten by the firm.
Merrill Lynch spokesman Timothy Gilles said the firm had no comment on the reports of the Wells notice. But he added; "We are confident our disclosure was proper."
A Wells notice informs its recipient that SEC staff intends to recommend enforcement action to commissioners.
SEC officials in Los Angeles and Washington were not immediately available to comment on the investigation. In the past, SEC officials have refused to comment.
Orange County attorney Bruce Bennett said the developments were not a surprise.

"This is not unexpected," Bennett said. "During the commission's investigation of the county, it made clear it was concerned about the disclosure made in connection with the county's 1994 ($600 million) taxable note issue underwritten by Merrill."

Orange County filed for protection under Chapter 9 of the federal Bankruptcy Code on December 6, 1994, after investment losses of more than $1.6 billion. The county emerged from bankruptcy in June of this year.
The bankruptcy stunned the nation and the municipal bond market because the southern California county had long been considered a bastion of wealth and stability.
Following the bankruptcy filing, the SEC initiated a sweeping investigation of the county's risky borrowings.

Based on its investigation of the crisis, the SEC filed complaints against the former county Treasurer Robert Citron and former Assistant Treasurer Matthew Raabe earlier this year, alleging they made misleading statements in the offer and sale of more than $2.1 billion of municipal securities.
As previously reported, SEC staff has sent Wells notices to several municipalities, including the the cities of Irvine and Anaheim, and several local school districts.

Several firms besides Merrill Lynch have also received Wells notices, including CS First Boston Corp. Last week it was disclosed that Jean Costanza, a partner with the law firm of LeBoeuf Lamb Greene & MacRae, had received a Wells.

Meanwhile, in a bid to recover the funds it lost, Orange County has sued Merrill Lynch, McGraw-Hill Cos Inc.'s Standard & Poor's Corp., Morgan Stanley Group Inc., KPMG Peat Marwick LLP, the Student Loan Marketing Association, LeBoeuf Lamb Greene & MacRae and financial firm Rauscher Pierce Refsnes Inc.
Earlier this week, the county added a $120-million-plus lawsuit against Fuji Securities Inc. for its alleged involvement in the county's financial collapse.
Merrill Lynch has denied any wrongdoing and asserts that county officials were responsible for the financial losses. The other firms are also fighting the county lawsuits.
